en: *Samayabhedoparacanacakra*, one fascicle,
composed by the Great Bodhisattva Vasumitra;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples’ adherence to divergent sects impaired the Tathāgata’s true teaching and the benefit of sentient beings;
because they clung to the literal meaning of the *neyārtha* (provisional) sūtras, they fell into error.
Arousing weariness and fear in sentient beings, I shall now explain, based on reason and scripture, the Great Bodhisattva Devamitra.
Contemplating suffering, he gave rise to a vast vow, supreme wisdom, meditative concentration, and a compassionate mind; thus he reflected upon this meaning.
Seeing all sentient beings flowing along with various views,
I have taught the meaning of reality as it is revealed by the Buddha’s words.
If one understands the Buddha’s true teaching, the Noble Truths will be its foundation.
Therefore, one should grasp the truth, just like gold within the sand;
such is what was heard after the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, had passed into parinirvāṇa.
When a full hundred years have passed—
just as the bright sun has hidden behind Mount Aṣṭāpada—
and sixteen years have further elapsed beyond that century.
There was a great kingdom named Pāṭaliputra.
Its king was named Aśoka,
who ruled over Jambudvīpa.
There was a great white canopy covering one world-system.
At such a time, the great assembly dispersed;
there are four kinds of ways in which a great assembly may disperse.
First, the assembly of a great kingdom;
second, the assembly of outsiders;
third, the assembly of those who have heard much; fourth, the assembly of the virtuous elders.
These four great assemblies together expounded the five kinds of causal conditions established by the non-Buddhists.
As for these five causal conditions:
As stated in that verse:
"The defiled garments of others— [those] manifested by ignorance, doubt,
and the words of those who have transcended the Noble Path— these are the true teachings of the Buddhas."
Upon careful examination of these five points,
they were divided into two schools:
first, the Mahāsāṃghika.
The second is the Sthavira school of disciples;
by the second century [after the parinirvāṇa],
it branched from the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Furthermore, three sections emerge:
first, the Exposition of the Sections;
second, the Exposition of the Supramundane.
The third is the Haimavata school.
During this second century,
another school emerged from the Mahāsāṃghika.
They are called the Bahuśrutīya school.
During this second century [after the Buddha's passing],
another school emerged from the Mahāsāṃghika.
It was called the Vibhajyavāda school.
When this second century had been completed,
there was a non-Buddhist practitioner.
His name was Mahādeva;
he went forth among the Mahāsāṃghika school and dwelt alone in the mountains.
It is taught that the Mahāsāṃghika school split into two sub-sects due to five points of doctrinal disagreement.
First, the Caitika school;
second, the Uttaraśaila school.
Thus, the Mahāsāṃghika school underwent four schisms and five schisms.
These were combined into seven schools:
first, the Mahāsāṃghika;
second, the Ekavyāvahārika.
3. The Lokottaravādins; 4. The Pūrvaśailas; 5. The Bahulikas.
Sixth, the Vibhajyavāda school;
seventh, the Caitīya school;
and the Uttaraśaila school.
The school of the Elder Disciples (Sthaviravāda) shall remain in the world for a thousand years;
by the middle of its third century, [it will reach this point].
Due to minor causes and conditions, they split into two schools: the Sarvāstivāda,
also known as the Hetuvāda.
Second is the Haimavata school,
also known as the Sthavira-śiṣya school;
it arose during this third century [after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa].
From the Sarvāstivāda school,
another sect emerged,
called the Kaukkutika (or Kukkutika) school.
During this third century,
four further schools emerged from the Kaukkutika branch of disciples.
1. Ekavyāvahārika; 2. Bahuśrutīya; 3. Sammitīya.
The Caturthīya (Four Forest-Dwelling) school [arose] from the Sarvāstivāda during this third century.
Furthermore, another school emerged,
named the Saṃmatīya, during this third century.
From the Sāmmitīya school,
another school emerged,
named the Dharmaguptaka.
This school declares that Mugalan is their own Great Teacher.
During this third century, [they] branched from the Sarvāstivāda school.
Furthermore, another school emerged,
named the Śāṇavāsinīya,
also known as the Kauṇḍinyaśiṣyaka.
During the fourth century,
another school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda.
They are called the Sautrāntika school,
also known as the Sūtravādin school;
such are the schools of the Śrāvaka disciples of the Sthavira.
Combined, they are divided into eleven schools:
first, the Sarvāstivāda; second, the Haimavata.
Third, the Kṣāntivādin branch;
fourth, the Dharmottarīya branch;
fifth, the Bhadrayānīya branch.
6. The Saṃmitīya school; 7. The Vanavāsī school;
8. The Mahīśāsaka school.
The ninth is the Dharmaguptaka school;
the tenth is the Kāśyapīya school;
the eleventh is the Mahīśāsaka school—these schools are the fundamental sources for holding to specific tenets.
There are differences in their interpretations of the meaning.
I shall now explain the fundamental basis of these interpretations:
the Mahāsāṃghika school.
The Ekavyāvahārikas, the Lokottaravādins,
and the Aparaseliyas.
These four schools constitute the fundamental basis for the interpretation of the meaning.
These various schools teach that all Buddha-Bhagavāns appear in the world.
There is not a single dharma of the Tathāgata that is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Every word uttered by the Tathāgata serves to turn the wheel of Dharma.
With a single voice, the Tathāgata can expound all dharmas.
The Tathāgata’s speech never fails to accord with the truth.
The Tathāgata’s form-body is boundless.
The Tathāgata’s majestic power and influence never diminish.
The lifespan of the Tathāgata is boundless.
The Tathāgata teaches and transforms sentient beings,
causing them to give rise to joyful faith and a mind of insatiable diligence.
The Tathāgata is always free from sleep;
the Tathāgata provides answers to questions without deliberation;
such are the words uttered by the Tathāgata.
They cause all sentient beings to give rise to a mind of love and joy.
The Tathāgata’s mind always abides in contemplation, tranquil and unmoving.
With a single mind, the Tathāgata is able to penetrate all realms of experience.
The Tathāgata’s prajñā associated with a single kṣaṇa can understand all dharmas;
this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising.
They always act with impartiality in accordance with the mind,
even until they reach nirvana without remainder.
All bodhisattvas likewise enter the womb in this manner.
There is no kalala, arbuda, or peśī.
Gahanaśakha, Parāśaka, Kīśalomanākha, and so forth.
When a bodhisattva is about to enter the womb,
he always manifests the appearance of a white elephant.
When the bodhisattva emerges from the womb...
All were born from the mother’s right side.
All bodhisattvas are free from thoughts of greed and free from thoughts of anger.
He has no intention to afflict others.
If a bodhisattva makes a vow to be reborn in the evil realms,
he will attain rebirth there by the power of that vow.
The Bodhisattva enters the evil realms for the purpose of teaching and bringing sentient beings to maturity;
he accepts this birth not because he is bound by the fetters of afflictions and karma,
but because he single-mindedly and correctly contemplates the Four Noble Truths.
One wisdom penetrates the four noble truths as well as the characteristics of the four noble truths.
Within the five consciousnesses, there is both defiled and pure form.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are likewise the six aggregates of consciousness;
the five sense organs are merely masses of flesh,
and the eye does not see forms.
Even to the point where the body does not perceive touch,
if the mind is in meditative concentration,
there can still be speech; thus, the subduing of the mind is ever-present.
The mind that destroys appearances is ever-present;
therefore, ordinary beings have higher and lower states.
Once the Dharma is fully accomplished, it has no location.
Sudatta: "The mind and mental factors possess an intrinsic nature."
There are Arhats who stain their robes with impurities;
there are many Arhats who possess ignorance;
there are those who have doubts and those who rely on others for guidance.
The Noble Path is likewise revealed by words;
it is described as suffering,
and it is also described as the cause.
Prajñā is associated with the cessation of suffering;
the sensation of suffering is also nutriment;
and the eighth [dhyāna] also abides for a long time.
Up to the nature of the dharma of falling away;
the *sūtradārdha-paṇa* is the dharma of falling away;
the *arhattva* is the dharma of non-falling away.
In the world there is no right view;
in the world there is no faculty of faith;
there are no indeterminate phenomena.
If a person enters right concentration,
all fetters are extinguished;
this is called *sukkhavipassaka*.
One may commit all manner of evils,
provided only that one does not commit the five heinous crimes.
Among all the sutras, there is none that is not of provisional meaning.
There are nine kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*):
first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Third, the sphere of infinite space;
fourth, the sphere of infinite consciousness; fifth, the sphere of nothingness.
Sixth, the sphere of nothingness;
seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
eighth, the twelve factors of dependent origination.
The nine factors of the noble path;
the mind is pure by nature but defiled by adventitious stains;
and the single latent affliction.
The two types of afflictions— those that arise manifestly and those that are latent—
are neither mind nor mental factors, and they lack an object of perception.
Latent proclivities (anuśaya) are distinct from manifest afflictions (paryavasthāna).
Latent proclivities are dissociated from the mind, whereas manifest afflictions are associated with the mind.
The past and the future do not exist as the present; yet they are dharmas that enter into the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
It is neither an object of knowledge nor an object of cognition.
The intermediate state (antarābhava) does not exist.
Sūtradharabhadra attained meditative concentration.
These four schools constitute the fundamental basis for their respective tenets.
Regarding differences in tenets:
the Mahāsāṃghika school maintains tenets that differ from those of the other three schools.
The Four Noble Truths are entirely real.
There is suffering corresponding to suchness that can be praised through practice;
this is the suffering produced by one's own actions.
There is suffering caused by oneself;
there is suffering caused by both [self and other];
there is suffering not caused by either.
They arise dependent on causes and conditions; some do not arise dependent on causes and conditions.
Within a single moment, many minds may conjoin, such that the path and the afflictions arise simultaneously.
Karma and its fruit arise simultaneously;
the seed is itself the sprout.
The six sense organs and the four great elements undergo transformation.
The mind and mental factors do not undergo transformation or change;
the mind pervades the body, and the body grows.
One should understand that there are such meanings as these.
The various schools have differing degrees of faith and inclination,
each maintaining its own tenets;
this is called "difference in the adherence to meanings."
The Mahīśāsaka school is the fundamental authority for these tenets.
The Tathāgata’s five proclamations should be explained;
as for the five proclamations concerning the supramundane:
That is to say: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the tranquility of nirvāṇa—these five sounds constitute the supramundane path.
Any other sounds of the Tathāgata are mundane paths.
There are Arhats who defile their robes with impurities;
there are many Arhats who possess ignorance and harbor doubt.
There is another [school] that holds that the Noble Path is also manifested by words;
their other tenets are similar to those held by the Sarvāstivādins.
The Vibhajyavāda school maintains that suffering is not the aggregates (skandhas). This is the fundamental tenet of their doctrine.
All bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are unestablished.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are designated as "suffering" because they are established through mutual dependence and conceptual designation;
they possess no power of an agent.
There is no such thing as untimely death;
everything obtained is produced by previously created karma.
It is the growth of causes and conditions that gives rise to karma.
All sufferings arise from karma;
the Noble Path is attained through merit.
The Noble Path is not attained through cultivation.
The tenets held by others are similar to those held by the Mahāsāṃghika school,
as well as the Caitīya school and the Uttaraśaila school.
These two sections are the fundamental basis for grasping the meaning.
A bodhisattva is not liberated from the evil realms;
within the swamp of afflictions, one may obtain a small measure of grasping through respectful service.
There are Arhats who defile their robes with impurities;
there are many Arhats who possess ignorance and harbor doubts.
There is another liberation;
the Noble Path is also expressed by words.
Other tenets held [by other schools] are similar to those held by the Mahāsāṃghikas.
The Sarvāstivāda school is the fundamental tenet of this doctrine.
"All exists" means that all things exist as they are;
these two principles—existence and suchness—comprehend all phenomena of the past, present, and future.
There is first reliance on correct teaching;
second, reliance on the two dharmas;
and third, reliance on that which possesses an objective sphere.
The four reliances have their fruits.
The sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) has three aspects:
that which is cognized, that which is known, and that which is penetrated.
Birth, aging, duration, and impermanence:
these formations are dissociated from the mind.
They are comprised within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) and constitute three types of conditioned phenomena.
There are three kinds of unconditioned phenomena,
three characteristics of conditioned phenomena, and three characteristics of unconditioned phenomena.
Among the Four Noble Truths, three truths are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and one truth is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
One contemplates these Four Noble Truths in their sequential order.
If a person wishes to enter right concentration,
they must take the gate of liberation of emptiness and the gate of liberation of wishlessness as their object;
only then can they enter right concentration.
If one contemplates the conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm,
one enters right concentration; once a person has entered right concentration,
they abide within fifteen moments of mind.
It is called the stage leading toward *srotāpanna*.
When one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind,
it is called *srotāpanna*.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) consists of a single moment of mind.
Regarding the three preparatory stages (*prayoga*), there is the possibility of regression; regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharma, there is no possibility of regression.
The *sūtradābhanna* has no sense of falling away;
Arhats, however, mostly have the sense of falling away.
This applies to all Arhats.
Most do not fully attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Even ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) can abandon desire and hatred,
and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) may attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
The gods also have the Brahmā realm;
in the seven meditative attainments (dhyāna), there are factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), whereas in other attainments, they do not exist.
All meditative concentrations (samādhi) are without exception subsumed within the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
If one does not rely on concentration to enter right concentration,
one may still attain arhatship, though for the most part this relies upon the minds of the form realm (rūpadhātu) and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
One may attain the state of an arhat without being able to enter right concentration.
Within the desire realm, one can both enter right concentration and attain the state of an arhat. This is also the case in Uttarakuru.
There are no people who have not abandoned desire;
noble ones are not born in that place,
nor are noble ones born in the Heaven of Non-conception.
The sequence is not fixed for attaining the four fruits of the noble path.
This applies if a person has already entered right concentration.
Based on the worldly path, one attains the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the stage of *anāgāmin*.
It may be said that all latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
All latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) that are not associated with the mind may be designated as "perversions" (*viparyāsa*).
All manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) may be designated by the term "perversion," but they cannot be designated by the term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
The twelvefold dependent origination is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The factors of the twelvefold dependent origination also exist;
they follow the predominant activity of the arhat,
and thus the arhat is predominant.
There is also an increase in merit.
Within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire and form realms,
the five consciousnesses arise manifestly.
At that time, desire arises;
one cannot be free from desire. The five consciousnesses grasp distinct objects and lack conceptual discrimination.
The mind and its concomitant mental factors (caitta), as well as the mind and its concomitant mental factors, necessarily possess objects.
A nature does not associate with itself;
the mind does not associate with itself.
In the world there is right view;
in the world there is the faculty of faith;
there are indeterminate phenomena.
Among arhats, there are none who possess the qualities of those still in training (śaikṣa-dharma).
While all arhats have attained concentration (samādhi),
not all arhats have realized [the fruit of] concentration.
Arhats often still receive retribution for their past karma;
likewise, all ordinary beings may die while in a virtuous state of mind.
However, if a person is in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they will certainly not die.
The Tathāgata and his disciples are no different in that their delusions have been extinguished;
the Tathāgata’s compassion does not take sentient beings as its objective domain.
If a person clings to the mark of a sentient being with the intention of seeking liberation,
they will not achieve the samādhis of all bodhisattvas;
such an ordinary person is possessed of the nine fetters.
If a bodhisattva has already entered right concentration but has not yet transcended the stage of ordinary beings,
this is the continuity of what is grasped as signs.
Sentient beings are merely provisional designations.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary;
there is no dharma that passes from this world to a future world.
Relying on worldly conventional designations,
one speaks of a *pudgala* who delivers others;
during the time of the True Dharma, the formations (*saṃskāra*) perish without remainder.
The aggregates (skandhas) are without change;
there is supramundane concentration (lokottara-samādhi);
and there are various thoughts (vitarka) that are untainted (anāsrava).
That which is wholesome has a cause.
When a person is in meditative absorption, there is no speech.
The Noble Eightfold Path is called the Wheel of Dharma.
Not all the speech of the World-Honored One constitutes the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
a single utterance does not fully expound all dharmas.
Not all speech corresponds to its meaning;
not all sūtras are of definitive meaning (nītārtha).
There are sūtras that are of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
The Sarvāstivādins take this principle as their fundamental tenet;
were there to be further adherence to divergent views, it would lead to an infinite regress.
The Himavat school is the fundamental tenet;
the bodhisattva is an ordinary person who has no craving for rebirth.
They are not enveloped by a womb or the like;
non-Buddhists do not possess the five supernormal powers;
and among the gods, there is no Māra.
There are Arhats who stain their robes with impurities;
there are many Arhats who possess ignorance and harbor doubts.
There is another school;
its noble path is also expressed by means of words,
and their other tenets are similar to those held by the Sarvāstivādins.
The Vātsīputrīya school maintains this as its fundamental tenet:
that the person is neither identical to the five aggregates nor distinct from the five aggregates.
Because they subsume the aggregates, elements, and sense bases,
provisional designations such as "person" are established.
There are three kinds of such provisional designations.
1. Subsuming all conventional designations;
2. Subsuming a portion of conventional designations;
3. Subsuming conventional designations that are subject to cessation.
All conditioned phenomena perish moment by moment.
Apart from form, there is not a single dharma that passes from this world to the next;
it can be said that there is no transmigrating person.
The non-Buddhists possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
If a person is currently generating the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*),
they are neither free from desire nor have they attained detachment from desire.
The various fetters associated with the desire realm that are abandoned through the path of cultivation—
if a person can sever these, they attain freedom from desire. It is not so,
however, for those [fetters] of the desire realm that are abandoned through the path of vision.
Patience (kṣānti) is called the Worldly Supreme Dharma (laukikāgradharma).
These four stages are termed "right concentration" (samyak-samādhi).
If a person has already entered right concentration...
Within the twelve moments of mind,
this is called the candidate for the *śuklārdhapakṣa*;
upon reaching the thirteenth moment of mind, it is named the *śuklārdhapakṣa*.
All sentient beings have two kinds of loss:
first, the loss of intention;
second, the loss of action.
There are two supreme causes of birth and death:
first, afflictions;
second, karma.
These two factors are the supreme causes for liberation:
namely, vipaśyanā and śamatha. If one does not rely on self-respect (*ātma-adhipati-pratyaya*) and a sense of shame (*hrī*), [liberation cannot be attained].
The True Dharma does not belong to such a person.
There are two kinds of roots of affliction that constantly follow the conduct of all sentient beings.
This refers to ignorance and craving for existence. There are seven bases of purification;
the Buddha’s wisdom is not associated with the precepts and so forth.
All objects, by means of their basis and the conditions through which they are cognized,
enable one to penetrate all phenomena;
if these are subsumed under cessation.
There are six types of beings who do not enter right concentration in the form and formless realms;
among them, bodhisattvas are always born, and once born,
they attain the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Thus one is named a Buddha.
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the sūtras has three meanings.
The first is to reveal the faults of saṃsāra.
Second, it reveals the merit of liberation.
Third, the *Sthavira-vāda* school maintains that this meaning is fundamental,
as it derives from a single verse concerning the original cause.
This section consists of four divisions:
namely, the Dharmottara-tantra and the Bhadrayāna-tantra.
The Saṃmitīya school and the Ghoṣaka school state in verse:
Having attained liberation, one falls back again; this falling occurs through attachment and one returns once more.
Having reached a state of peace, one wanders among pleasant things; because of acting according to desire, one arrives at a place of pleasure.
This is the fundamental meaning held by the Sammitīya school.
The past and future are non-existent; the present and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are existent.
These four noble truths are observed simultaneously. If one perceives the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya), [one perceives all four].
One immediately perceives all truths.
Having perceived them, one sees that the latent tendencies and afflictions toward those previously perceived truths are neither mind nor mental factors associated with the mind.
There is no objective sphere;
latent proclivities are one thing,
and manifestly active afflictions are another.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) are dissociated from the mind;
the manifest afflictions (paryavasthāna) are associated with the mind.
Ordinary persons do not abandon the desire for the realm of desire (kāmadhātu-rāga) and hatred (dveṣa), with the exception of [the latter] toward external objects.
The Path has no five supernormal powers;
the heavens have no Māra; and there is no intermediate state (antarābhava).
For an arhat, merit does not increase. The group of five consciousnesses is associated with defilement and dissociated [from it];
the group of six consciousnesses is associated with vitarka and vicāra.
At times there are beings who are like the headless;
the world lacks right view,
and the world lacks the faculty of faith.
There is no supramundane concentration;
there is no outflow-free state in vitarka and vicāra;
there is cause but no goodness.
The *sūtradārbhaṇa* possesses the quality of falling away (*parihāṇadharma*),
whereas the *arhat* generally does not possess the quality of falling away.
These factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are subsumed within the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
There are nine kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*):
first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Third, emptiness;
fourth, non-self;
fifth, the suchness of goodness.
Sixth, the suchness of the unwholesome;
seventh, the suchness of the indeterminate;
eighth, the suchness of the path.
The nine conditions give rise to suchness.
Birth is the beginning;
death and falling away are the end.
The four great elements, the five faculties,
the mind, and the mental factors that assist the mind all undergo transformation.
Within the great assembly there is the Buddha;
if one makes an offering to the great assembly, the retribution obtained is vast.
However, if one makes a separate offering to the Buddha, the merit does not equal that [of the former].
All Buddhas and all śrāvakas share the same path and the same liberation;
all conditioned phenomena are momentary.
There is not a single dharma that passes from this world to the next;
this is the fundamental tenet held by the Saṃmatīya school.
Furthermore, this school maintains another distinct doctrine.
Regarding the dharmas of the intermediate state (antarābhava) existing in the past and future,
there are two kinds: that which is known and that which is cognized through mental attention (manasikāra).
This is right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
There are no two separate actions of body and speech;
initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) are associated mental factors (*samprayukta-dharma*).
The great earth remains for an eon;
one serves the shrines and ponds with reverence, yet there is no karmic retribution;
all latent proclivities and afflictions persist constantly.
The three phenomena of the present— aggregates, elements, and sense bases— are ever-present.
Regarding the present phenomenon of dissociation,
the verse says:
These five factors are determinative; from them all sufferings arise:
ignorance, the mind, craving, the five views, and all karmic actions.
The fundamental meaning of these various sections is entirely the same.
Because they maintained that there was a distinction [between the Buddha and the Dharma], they formed a separate school.
The Dharmaguptaka school is the fundamental source of this doctrinal tenet:
that within the Saṃgha there exists the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
By relying on the Shudou Reservoir and giving rise to reverence, one receives a superior reward;
yet this does not equal the merit of revering the Great Assembly.
The path of the Buddha is distinct, and the path of the śrāvakas is distinct.
The non-Buddhists do not possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Arhats have many bodies that are free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
Other points they maintain are similar to those maintained by the Mahāsāṃghika school.
The Bhadrayānīya school:
this is the fundamental tenet;
the dharmas themselves are that which is to be extinguished.
That which has already been abandoned is non-existent;
that which has not yet been extinguished or abandoned exists.
If the fruit of karma has already matured, it is non-existent.
